transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you; could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Hey Dr. Smith. Yeah, so, I came in because... man, I just feel like I’m literally crawling out of my skin whenever I’m supposed to sit still. Like in the radiology suite or in my classes. Which, honestly, the classes are crazy long. We had this one professor last week who brought in these physical bone models, and the room smelled so weird, kind of like dust and old chemicals? I don't know why they can't just use digital stuff, my laptop has this insane 3D program that renders everything way better. I built my PC myself, actually, got a new graphics card for it and everything so it runs super smooth. 

But anyway, yeah, I've been trying to just tough it out for months now, but I just can't do it. I always end up pacing around the room, or just shifting in my chair constantly, or finding some random excuse to get up and move. Like I'll pretend I need to check the inventory in the supply closet... which is a total mess right now, by the way, someone left a bunch of contrast dye boxes right in the middle of the floor and I almost tripped over them on Tuesday...
Have you struggled with this kind of restlessness or difficulty sitting still since you were a child, or is this something that started more recently?

Oh, definitely since I was a kid. Like, my parents still talk about my elementary school parent-teacher conferences. The teachers were always complaining that I was constantly out of my seat, or calling out answers, or just rushing ahead before they even finished giving directions. 

Which, honestly, I hate directions. Even now, if I buy something, I just look at the picture on the box and start building. I helped my buddy put together this TV stand last weekend, and he was trying to read the manual step-by-step, and I'm just like, dude, give me the screws, it's obvious. We actually ended up putting the back panel on backwards, but you can't even tell because it's against the wall. His apartment is so tiny anyway, and it's right next to the train tracks, so the whole place literally shakes when the freight trains go by at night. It's crazy loud. 

But yeah, what was I saying? Oh, right, so this was happening way before middle school. It's definitely not just something that started recently with my radiology training.

Looking back at your time in school, did you frequently struggle with losing your school supplies, forgetting to turn in assignments, or having trouble staying focused on tasks that didn't interest you?

Honestly, no, not really? Like, I didn't really lose my stuff. I actually always buy these very specific pens—the Pilot G2s, but only the 0.38 millimeter ones because the thicker ones smear everywhere and it drives me absolutely crazy. My buddy Jake is left-handed and he literally can't use them because he drags his hand across the paper when he writes. It's so weird to watch. He actually broke his wrist snowboarding last winter, and I got to see his X-rays when I was doing my clinical rotation. The distal radius fracture was just gnarly. They had to put in, like, all these titanium plates and screws, which look super cool on a radiograph, by the way. Titanium doesn't cause as much artifact on an MRI either, which is good because his girlfriend works at an imaging center downtown and... wait. What were we talking about? 

Oh, right, assignments and stuff. Yeah, no, I didn't really forget to turn things in. I usually just rushed through them as fast as humanly possible so I could go do something else. I never really spaced out or lost focus like I was daydreaming, I just hated being stuck in the chair doing it.
Looking back at your childhood, would you say you frequently acted without thinking, such as blurting out answers in class or interrupting others while they were talking?

Yeah, oh man, all the time. Still do, honestly. Like, even now at the clinic, when a supervisor is explaining a positioning step for a scan, or asking me a question about the protocol, I’ll just jump in with the answer before they even finish talking. And then I realize I completely missed the part that actually mattered, because they were asking something else entirely. It's so embarrassing. 

But it's just like... I know the answer! Or I think I do. It's like my brain is already ten steps ahead. Speaking of being ten steps ahead, I was trying to explain this new leveling system in this MMO I'm playing to my brother, and he just could not keep up. He plays a healer class, which I think is so boring. You just stand in the back and watch health bars go up and down. I have to play DPS, like a rogue or something, where I'm constantly moving and doing combos. If I'm not mashing buttons, I literally fall asleep at the keyboard. I actually spilled an entire energy drink on my mechanical keyboard last month because I fell asleep during a raid. It was a nightmare to clean. I had to take off every single keycap and swab the switches with rubbing alcohol. The alcohol smelled exactly like the prep wipes we use at the clinic before starting an IV... wait, what was the question? Did I answer it?
In your daily life now, outside of the physical restlessness, do you often find that you make careless mistakes in your work because you aren't paying close enough attention to the details?

Careless mistakes? I mean, not really? Like, I wouldn't say I make mistakes because I'm not paying attention to the details. If anything, I'm just doing it too fast, you know? But I don't really mess up the actual work. Like, when I'm setting up for an X-ray, I know exactly what I'm doing. The positioning, the angles—it's all muscle memory at this point. 

Which is wild, because muscles actually have this thing called muscle memory, but it's really just your nervous system building pathways. I was reading about this guy who lost his arm, but he still felt like he could move his fingers. Phantom limb syndrome. It's fascinating how the brain just... keeps expecting the input. Kind of like how I keep expecting my car to start on the first try, but the starter motor has been whining for like three weeks. I know I need to take it in, but the mechanic I go to is all the way across town, and there's always so much traffic on I-95. The last time I was stuck there, I saw this guy in a convertible trying to eat a bowl of cereal while driving. Like, an actual ceramic bowl with milk. Who does that? What happens if you hit a pothole? You're just wearing Cheerios for the rest of the day. 

But yeah, I don't really think I make careless mistakes at work. I just... do things fast. Did that make sense?
